item.title: Never Open the Utility App Again: The Complete Beginner's Guide to Integrating State Grid into Home Assistant (Zero-Loss Restarts & Automated Alerts)
item.description:
Anyone managing a smart home has experienced the same anxiety: during scorching summer heatwaves or freezing winter nights, heaters and air conditioners run around the clock, leaving you wondering how much electricity was consumed yesterday and whether your prepaid balance is about to run out.

Historically, the only option was tedious: open a sluggish commercial utility app on your smartphone, sit through splash screens and slow loading spinners, and manually check an isolated balance figure. Worse, if an unexpected zero-balance blackout occurs in the middle of the night, refrigerators shut down and expensive perishables spoil before anyone notices.

The true value of a smart home is not shifting physical remotes into smartphone screens; it is making essential household indicators work autonomously for your family. Having yesterday’s kilowatt-hours, real-time prepaid balance, and monthly comparisons visible on a wall-mounted dashboard—or receiving an automated gentle voice alert from smart speakers and instant notifications via mobile apps whenever balance drops below 50 CNY—is where practical home automation truly shines.

This guide provides a step-by-step, zero-confusion walkthrough designed specifically for Home Assistant beginners. Whether you have just set up your first Home Assistant server or have struggled in the past with disappearing entities after system reboots, following this tutorial will get your State Grid integration running reliably in 15 minutes with permanent persistence safeguards.

item.title: Carrier Bills in Home Assistant Hit Error 3006: How an Agent Reverse-Engineered China Telecom Protocols for a Zero-Cloud Device Auth
item.description:

Exploring community forums revealed two common workarounds: either hoping for elusive cellular gateway silent logins, or submitting phone numbers, service PINs, and one-time SMS verification codes to shadowy third-party cloud proxy services. Today, I instructed a local AI Agent to reverse-engineer China Telecom official authentication protocols: from probing why home broadband WiFi cannot trigger silent cellular tokens, to hand-coding a pure in-memory, zero-cloud LAN authorization server; from using offscreen Canvas alpha scanning to eliminate slider puzzle visual offsets, to restructuring the Home Assistant integration lifecycle to fix startup crashes and concurrency locks.

Here is the full retrospective of an engineering journey that bridged carrier security barriers with private smart home automation.

item.title: A Single Click Broke All Three Midea Appliances: Escaping Home Assistant's 6-Minute Boot Freeze with Offline Dependency Injection
item.description:
The most heart-stopping moment in smart home administration is never unboxing a finicky new sensor. It is watching a core integration that has run smoothly for months flash a bright update prompt in HACS. You casually hit “Update,” reboot the server, and watch in disbelief as your appliances vanish, while the entire smart home hub locks up mid-boot.

On October 26, 2026, I performed an upgrade assessment and deployment for the Midea AC LAN integration on our local Home Assistant hub, which governs our household drum washing machine, smart dishwasher, and gas water heater. Transitioning from v2026.9.1 to v2026.10.0 seemed like an ordinary patch. Instead, it triggered a series of critical bottlenecks: an agonizing boot freeze exceeding six minutes, all three core appliances falling into a red “Not Loaded” state, sweeping breaking changes in device entity schemas, and a dependency resolution stall under degraded network connectivity.

This article provides a comprehensive field review of the nearly two-hour diagnostic deep dive. It includes detailed symptom analysis, architectural code archaeology, everyday analogies, a zero-patch offline healing blueprint verified in production, and one-click automation scripts tailored for Windows 11, Ubuntu 26.04, and macOS 27.

item.title: Migrated My NAS Static Site from Web Station to an nginx Container and Hit the ACL Wall
item.description:
Short answer first: the scariest part of this migration was not that the container failed to start, and not that port 80/443 was difficult to switch.

The real problem was that the site files were mounted into the container, nginx was running, and yet the pages still would not load.

In the end, the root cause was not a bad path, not a bad nginx config, and not a broken image. It was the Synology permission model: Unix permissions were only the front gate, while ACL acted like an extra access list. The nginx worker inside the container simply was not on the allowed list.

So this post is not just about replacing Web Station with an nginx container. It is about a more useful lesson: when containerizing a NAS static site, think carefully about who is allowed to read the files before you obsess over the web server config.

item.title: Home Assistant Had My Electricity Bill. Then I Restarted It.
item.description:
I wanted one small addition to my Home Assistant dashboard: how much electricity the household used each day.

An Agent installed the collector. I entered the credentials myself. The second CAPTCHA attempt succeeded, and the collector pushed the electricity data into HA. Six summary tiles and a daily list appeared. It looked finished.

Another configuration task then restarted Home Assistant. Several electricity tiles changed to “Entity not found.”

The useful part of these two days was discovering that successful login, a visible number, restart recovery and durable history are four separate acceptance tests.

item.title: 674 Entities, 157 “Unavailable”: Two Days of Giving Home Assistant a Proper Cleanup with Agents
item.description:
A smart home can become strangely difficult to use. Every room has sensors, every appliance has an integration, yet opening the dashboard still leaves you wondering where the right switch went.

On October 25, 2026, I asked an Agent to perform a read-only audit of my Home Assistant installation. It found 674 state entities, 157 marked unavailable, and 126 with unknown states. Weather had stopped producing useful data. Old automations referenced sensors whose physical purpose had changed. A retired robot vacuum still had an entire configuration surrounding it.

Over the following day, appliances, electricity data, wireless networking and infrastructure monitoring joined the system. Connecting them was only part of the work. Their capabilities needed useful places: everyday controls within reach, faults somewhere visible, and a sensible explanation when an action was temporarily unavailable.

This is the account of that cleanup, including several things that looked finished until a different acceptance check revealed another problem.

item.title: The Master Key Was Literally '4'? How Two Ground-Level Security Flaws Almost Broke the Internet This Week
item.description:
The Executive Summary

If the modern internet were a bustling metropolis, HTTPS certificates would serve as the official notary seals on every skyscraper doorway, while backend server runtimes act as the master chefs cooking up digital services inside every building.

Over the past seven days, the bedrock beneath this digital metropolis shuddered from two historic events:

First, eMudhra, an internationally recognized Certificate Authority (CA), experienced an operational failure during an offline key generation ceremony. Instead of generating elliptic curve private keys that are mathematically harder to guess than counting every atom in the observable universe, a flawed script produced intermediate CA keys with only 3 to 8 bits of entropy. One of these active private signing keys was literally calculated to be the single-digit integer 4.

Second, the PHP engine, which drives over 75% of the world’s web applications and server backends, disclosed PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), a critical 9.8-rated Remote Code Execution flaw that lets unauthenticated attackers hijack servers simply by sending an abnormal data payload.

Fortunately, major browser and OS vendors moved at record speed to deploy emergency blocks. This article provides a comprehensive, easy-to-understand breakdown of what happened, how it affects everyday users, and provides automated verification scripts and AI Agent procedures across Windows 11, Ubuntu 26.04, and macOS 27.

item.title: Free MiniMax Accounts, fnOS, and Daily Review: What's New in My Family's AI Notebook
item.description:
An AI mistake notebook can have a surprisingly technical first homework assignment: connect the AI before you can ask it about the child’s actual homework.

An API key, an endpoint and a model name are familiar settings to a developer. To a parent who wants to photograph a maths question and understand the mistake, they can feel like being asked to study a library’s computer system before borrowing a book.

The latest version of wrong-notebook, the open-source application I use with my own child and keep improving through use, removes part of that setup. Its new MiniMax Code OAuth channel lets a parent authorize a MiniMax Code account in the browser and use available account credits, including free credits, without first configuring an open-platform API key. The default model is MiniMax-M3.1-Flash.

There are useful changes beyond connecting a model: a list of questions due for review today, a way to return to yesterday’s unfinished practice, stricter answer checking, and backups that carry more of the learning history between devices.

item.title: Stop Copying Mistakes. Start Learning from Them: The AI Notebook I Use with My Child
item.description:
The easiest part of a mistake notebook is putting a question into it. The part that often falls apart is opening it a few days later and finding out whether your child can actually solve it now.

There is a question to copy, a diagram to redraw and an answer to organize. Once everything is neatly collected, the next review session starts with another search. If the same question goes wrong again, there may simply be another photograph, with little connecting the two attempts.

I have been using wrong-notebook with my own child for a while, and I keep refining it around this everyday workflow: let the computer handle more recognition, organization and retrieval, leaving the parent and child more attention for understanding and practice.

First, credit where it belongs. This project is a fork of wttwins/wrong-notebook. I am grateful for that foundation. My branch adds features and fixes around our family use, with the changes publicly available. It is already being used, and it will continue to change as new problems appear.

item.title: A VM Could Not Contain It: How a Deferred Checksum Became CVE-2026-99999, PwnEscape
item.description:
Running untrusted code in a virtual machine remains a useful security boundary. But every host interface that the guest can reach must also withstand untrusted input.

CVE-2026-99999, disclosed in October 2026 and named PwnEscape by its researchers, makes that qualification concrete. The vulnerable component was Linux networking. A checksum operation deferred for performance could change an IPv4 header after earlier processing had already validated it, undermining the guest-to-host boundary.

The evidence needs careful wording: Vercel confirmed host-memory disclosure in production sandboxes. Host crashes and complete host execution were demonstrated on researcher-owned KVM and Firecracker environments. This article reviews public sources and the patch; it does not claim an exploit was run against production systems.

item.title: We Guessed Wrong: Space Bunny Was Never Kimi. After 200 Trillion Anonymous Tokens, MiniMax M3.1 Flash Takes Off the Mask
item.description:

Today we got the answer: I was wrong.

On October 19, 2026, MiniMax published its MiniMax M3.1 Flash launch post, and the second paragraph says: “Space Bunny, which processed more than 200 trillion tokens while operating anonymously, was an early version of MiniMax M3.1 Flash.” The OpenRouter page that used to say stealth now carries a yellow banner: this stealth model was developed and operated by MiniMax, revealed to be MiniMax M3.1 Flash.

This post does three things. It lays out the bunny’s 27-day story, it owns up to why we guessed wrong and how community detectives guessed right, and it looks at the release’s benchmarks, price and usage to see whether it is worth switching.

item.title: The Container Said Up 4 Weeks, the Site Said 530: How QUIC Quietly Knocked My Cloudflare Tunnel Offline
item.description:
The confusing part of this outage was that everything I could see looked healthy.

The download site answered 200 in 8 ms from inside the LAN. The cloudflared container that publishes it said Up 4 weeks in docker ps. From the internet, though, the browser showed a single line, error code: 1033, with HTTP status 530.

The container was alive, but every tunnel connection inside it had dropped. The trigger was intermittent timeouts on the UDP 7844 egress that QUIC depends on. The amplifier was a two-year-old connector that tried to fall back to http2 and shut itself down instead.

item.title: 41 Free Online Logic Puzzles: A Quick Guide to the puzzle-*.com Series
item.description:

I found it by accident while looking for a Pipes game, then clicked through the banners at the bottom of the page one by one and realized it is a remarkably complete universe of logic puzzles. This post sorts all 41 by mechanic, shows each one’s official thumbnail with a one-line rule, and suggests a path for beginners.

item.title: DNS Answered in 1 ms and Sent Me to the Wrong Place: Three SmartDNS and AdGuard Home Traps
item.description:
The misleading part of this incident was that DNS kept answering.

The service was running, its ports were reachable, domestic sites resolved, and some queries took zero or one millisecond. The returned addresses told a different story: several overseas names pointed to unrelated destinations. Switching to a second DNS entry did not fix them.

The eventual repair crossed three layers: explicit domain routing, a verified overseas DoH path, and a CONNECT target compatibility issue between SmartDNS 47.1 and the existing proxy. Cache cleanup and client checks came afterward.

item.title: Free ISP IPTV Gathering Dust for Two Years? One Virtual Cable Put 112 Live Channels on Every Screen at Home (Shanghai Telecom, Tested)
item.description:
The short version

Your fiber modem (ONT) is very likely already passing the IPTV network down the cable. Nobody is picking it up. That was exactly my case: no ONT changes, no set-top-box credentials, no changes to the main router. I hot-plugged one VLAN 85 tagged virtual NIC into my side router on Proxmox VE, installed a small service called rtp2httpd, and every phone, TV and laptop at home can now watch the 112 live channels of Shanghai Telecom IPTV, with the first frame after a channel switch arriving in about 0.04 seconds.

I will explain VLANs, multicast and FCC with everyday analogies (parcel sorting, radio stations, catching a bus by taxi), show the evidence and real screenshots for each step, and finish with one-click scripts for Windows 11 / Ubuntu 26.04 / macOS 27 (tested for both apply and rollback), plus a guard-railed playbook for handing the job to an AI agent.
